title: Handling 200 Emails a Day as a Founder
summary: A realistic system for handling 200 emails a day as a founder, with real time-cost data, an EA-vs-AI cost comparison, and what actually changes by day 30.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


Two hundred emails a day is a volume problem, not a discipline problem. The realistic system is an AI-sorted inbox that labels mail into Important, Calendar, Billing, Newsletter, Order, Other and Work so only the threads that need you surface, plus drafts that improve by day 30. This guide has the time-cost math, an EA-versus-AI cost comparison, and what still needs a human.


Two hundred emails a day is not a discipline problem, it is a volume problem, and no amount of inbox-zero technique fixes volume. The fix is treating most of that mail as noise to be sorted automatically, so the handful of messages that actually need your judgment surface on their own. Below is what that looks like in practice, with real time-cost numbers rather than productivity-blog guesses.


Founders do not get 200 emails a day because they are disorganized. They get it because a startup routes investor updates, customer questions, hiring threads, and vendor logistics through one address with nobody else to triage it. Treating that inbox like a to-do list you clear by hand is how a founder loses an hour or two of building time daily to a task that does not require a founder.


## How much time does 200 emails a day actually cost?


The McKinsey Global Institute's widely cited analysis of knowledge-worker time puts email at about 28% of the workweek, roughly 2.6 hours a day. Founders running their own inbox tend to land at the higher end of that range or above it. In Slashy's own customer conversations, one early-stage founder described spending "more than 2 hours just answering emails" before automating triage and drafts, and said it now takes him "maybe ten minutes because everything's already sorted and there are drafts." That is not a hypothetical improvement; it is one founder's before-and-after on the same inbox.

## How does Slashy actually cut the number down?


Slashy does not reduce how much mail arrives. It reduces how much of it needs you. Inbound mail gets auto-labeled into categories like Important, Calendar, Billing, Newsletter, and Work, so the threads that move the company forward surface first instead of getting buried between a shipping notification and a newsletter. The in-house memory system drafts replies in your tone for one-click send, and it gets sharper the more it sees: acceptance climbs from around 30% on day 1 to 80%+ by day 30 as it learns your writing style, response timing, and who you talk to most.


Follow-up reminders with ghost detection catch what manual triage misses. When an outbound thread goes quiet past the window you would normally expect a reply, Slashy flags it instead of letting it sink. Open tracking shows who opened your email, on which device, and how many times, so a non-reply from a warm lead reads differently than one from someone who never opened the message at all.

## Does this replace hiring an executive assistant?


It moves the point at which hiring one makes sense, rather than removing it. The national average base salary for an executive assistant in the US is $64,456 a year as of mid-2026 per ZipRecruiter, before the 20 to 30 percent that payroll tax and benefits typically add. Most of what fills an EA's early days is triage: reading everything, drafting replies that do not need a founder's specific voice, chasing quiet threads, and finding a meeting time across calendars. That is the exact work an AI inbox is built to absorb.


Slashy handles the repeatable parts (sorting, first-pass drafts, ghost detection, calendar booking from the sidebar) at $300 a year on the Professional tier, well below a five-figure EA cost, let alone six. What it does not do is the work that actually needs a person: reading the room in a tense negotiation, rebooking a multi-leg trip on the fly mid-collapse, or a judgment call that depends on relationship context no software has. An AI inbox and an EA are not mutually exclusive; the AI inbox just moves back the date you need the second one.


## What happens to the emails that still need you?


They get louder, not quieter. Auto-labeling and drafting exist specifically to clear the routine 80% so the remaining 20% (a term sheet, an angry customer, a hire deciding between two offers) does not get lost in volume. Follow-up reminders make sure those threads do not go cold just because a reply required more than a one-click send. The goal is not an empty inbox. It is knowing that what is left in it actually needs you.
